seoTitle: How to Do MLA Format in Google Docs (2026)
metaDescription: Set up MLA format in Google Docs: margins, font, double spacing, the surname-and-page-number running head, and a proper hanging indent for Works Cited using the current menu paths.
intro:
MLA format is a handful of small rules applied consistently: one-inch margins, a readable 12-point font, double spacing everywhere, your surname and page number in the top-right corner, and a Works Cited list with hanging indents. None of it is hard in Google Docs. Most mistakes come from Docs defaults that quietly disagree with MLA, like Arial 11 as the starting font, or a page-number menu that has moved since many older guides were written.

This guide sets everything up from a blank document, then covers Google's own MLA template for when you want a head start.

steps.heading: Start from a blank document in pages format
steps.body:
Open Google Docs and click Blank document in the starter row on the home screen. The Report, Resume and Letter templates in that row are not MLA layouts, so a blank page is the cleaner starting point for a manual setup.

Before typing anything, open File > Page setup and make sure the document uses Pages, not Pageless. Headers and page numbers do not exist in pageless format, and MLA needs both. While you are in Page setup, confirm all four margins read 1 inch.

image.caption: The Google Docs home screen, with Blank document and a row of general-purpose starter templates above your recent files.

steps.heading: Change the font and spacing before you type
steps.body:
New Google Docs files start in Arial 11. Switch to Times New Roman (or another plainly readable font your instructor accepts) at 12 point.

Next, open Format > Line & paragraph spacing and choose Double. In the same submenu, remove any extra space before or after paragraphs. MLA wants uniform double spacing, including the heading block and the Works Cited page, with no bonus gap between paragraphs. Setting all of this on an empty document means every line you type inherits it.

steps.heading: Add the running head
steps.body:
Go to Insert > Page elements > Page number and pick the option that places numbers top right on every page. Older guides and videos show this as Insert > Page numbers; Google has since moved it under Page elements.

Click into the header, place the cursor before the number, and type your last name followed by a single space, so it reads "Smith 1". No "p.", no hyphen, no period. MLA puts this running head on every page, including page 1, so leave Different first page unticked. The head should sit half an inch from the top of the page; you can check or set that distance under Format > Headers & footers.

steps.heading: Type the heading, title and body
steps.body:
On the first page, left-aligned, type four lines: your name, your instructor's name, the course, and the date. On the next line, center your title. Keep it in the same font and size as the text, with no bold, underlining or quotation marks (unless it contains the title of another work).

Switch back to left alignment for the body. Indent the first line of each paragraph half an inch, which is what the Tab key does by default. If your instructor asks for a separate cover page, MLA allows you to drop the four-line heading from page 1, but that is the exception.

steps.heading: Format the Works Cited page
steps.body:
Insert a page break (Insert > Break > Page break) so the list starts on a new page. Center the label Works Cited at the top, then list sources alphabetically, still double-spaced, with the same running head continuing in the corner.

For the hanging indent, select the whole list and open Format > Align & indent > Indentation options. Under Special indent choose Hanging, leave the value at 0.5 inches, and click Apply. The first line of each entry now sits at the margin and every following line is indented half an inch. Dragging ruler markers produces the same result, but the dialog is exact and easier to repeat when you add sources later.

steps.heading: Or start from Google's MLA template
steps.body:
Google's Template gallery (reached from the Docs home screen) has an Education section with a Report template labeled MLA next to APA options. It fills in the heading layout, spacing and running head for you, and you replace the placeholder text.

Check it against the settings above before submitting. Confirm the font, the spacing and that your own surname appears in the running head, since templates are easy to leave half-edited.

troubleshooting.problem: There is no page number option, or the header area will not open
troubleshooting.cause: The document is in pageless format. Google Docs does not support headers, footers or page numbers in pageless documents.
troubleshooting.fix: Switch to Pages under File > Page setup, then add the page numbers.

troubleshooting.problem: The running head is missing from page 1
troubleshooting.cause: Different first page is ticked in the header settings, or the page-number option chosen skips the first page.
troubleshooting.fix: Untick Different first page, or re-insert the number through Insert > Page elements > Page number with the option that includes the first page.

troubleshooting.problem: Double spacing looks uneven, with bigger gaps between paragraphs
troubleshooting.cause: Extra space before or after paragraphs is still switched on for some of the text.
troubleshooting.fix: Select all (Ctrl+A or Cmd+A) and remove the space before and after paragraphs in Format > Line & paragraph spacing.

faq.question: Does MLA require Times New Roman?
faq.answer: Not strictly. MLA asks for a readable font in a standard size, and Times New Roman at 12 point is the usual choice. Google Docs defaults to Arial 11, so change it either way.

faq.question: Does the first page get a page number?
faq.answer: Yes. The surname-and-number running head goes on every page, starting with page 1, and continues through the Works Cited page.

faq.question: Where did Insert > Page numbers go?
faq.answer: Google moved it. It is now Insert > Page elements > Page number.

faq.question: Do I need a title page?
faq.answer: No. MLA uses a four-line heading on the first page. Only add a cover page if your instructor asks for one, in which case you can leave the heading off page 1.
